title: Critics and the rise of rock
summary: He blames critics for pushing rock and for favoring small groups and soloists.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Critics have always been a pain. They lead us down dark alleys, I wish they didn't but they do and they're prejudiced.
Do you have anybody specific in mind?
Yes; a lot of them. I won't get into it because one is replaced by another. I think they're largely responsible for the overwhelming position rock got in today.

There's nothing wrong with rock except there's just too much of it. It can be there, it certainly is part of the scene, it's always been, but it's too much. It wiped out everything else because of it's commercialism.
I think the record companies smelled money.
And decided to put all their merchandising behind it.

But the critics have been vociferous on small groups, on cultural heritage and soloistic gyration, which is fine, but not exclusively again. It needs something more than that, and the best players have something more than that.

It's kind of silly to think in terms of African folk music or Middle Eastern folk music outside of its context. It is true that we had a heritage of that; it came from the heritages we have, as a result of all the people who have come here. They brought it all with them and they put it all together and made a mish-mosh of it.
There's nothing wrong with that, but we are that, and I can see no reason to put it down, there is no reason to be ashamed or put it away. Other things come in and they are used too.
But to go exclusively for the hillbilly, the folk types of past ages, I don't go for that and I think the critics have had a lot to do with what has happened.
